name: "Array.prototype.sort()" and "Array.prototype.toSorted()" should use a compare function

descriptionSections.content:
JavaScript provides built-in methods to sort arrays, making it convenient for developers to manipulate data. There are two primary ways to sort an array:

  • Array.prototype.sort(): This method sorts the elements of an array in place and returns the sorted array.
  • Array.prototype.toSorted(): This method is designed to return a new sorted array, leaving the original array unchanged.

The default sort order is lexicographic (dictionary) order, based on the string representation of the elements. This means that when sorting an array of strings, numbers, or other elements, they are converted to strings and sorted according to their Unicode code points (UTF-16). For most cases, this default behavior is suitable when sorting an array of strings.

However, it’s essential to be aware of potential pitfalls when sorting arrays of non-string elements, particularly numbers. The lexicographic order may not always produce the expected results for numbers:

const numbers = [10, 2, 30, 1, 5];
numbers.sort(); // Noncompliant: lexicographic sort
console.log(numbers); // Output: [1, 10, 2, 30, 5]

To sort numbers correctly, you must provide a custom comparison function that returns the correct ordering:

const numbers = [10, 2, 30, 1, 5];
numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b);
console.log(numbers); // Output: [1, 2, 5, 10, 30]

Even to sort strings, the default sort order may give unexpected results. Not only does it not support localization, it also doesn’t fully support Unicode, as it only considers UTF-16 code units. For example, in the code below, "eΔ" is surprisingly before and after "éΔ". To guarantee that the sorting is reliable and remains as such in the long run, it is necessary to provide a compare function that is both locale and Unicode aware - typically String.localeCompare.

const code1 = '\u00e9\u0394'; // "éΔ"
const code2 = '\u0065\u0301\u0394'; // "éΔ" using Unicode combining marks
const code3 = '\u0065\u0394'; // "eΔ"
console.log([code1, code2, code3].sort()); // Noncompliant: ["éΔ", "eΔ", "éΔ"], "eΔ" position is inconsistent
console.log([code1, code2, code3].sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b))); // ["eΔ", "éΔ", "éΔ"]

Exceptions

This rule does not apply when two arrays of primitive values are sorted with the same method and then serialized before an equality or inequality comparison. In patterns such as JSON.stringify(a.sort()) === JSON.stringify(b.sort()) or JSON.stringify(a.toSorted()) !== JSON.stringify(b.toSorted()), sorting is only used to normalize element order before comparing the serialized values.

function haveSameElements(left, right) {
  return JSON.stringify(left.sort()) === JSON.stringify(right.sort());
}

function differ(left, right) {
  return JSON.stringify(left.toSorted()) !== JSON.stringify(right.toSorted());
}

Documentation

  • MDN web docs - Array.prototype.sort()
  • MDN web docs - Array.prototype.toSorted()
  • MDN web docs - String.prototype.localeCompare()

name: Literals should not be used for promise rejection

descriptionSections.content:
Documentation

  • typescript-eslint - Rule prefer-promise-reject-errors
  • MDN web docs - Promise
  • MDN web docs - Error

Related rules

  • S3696 - Literals should not be thrown

The use of literals (primitive values such as strings, numbers, booleans, etc.) for promise rejection is generally discouraged. While it is syntactically valid to provide literals as a rejected promise value, it is considered best practice to use instances of the Error class or its subclasses instead.

Using an instance of the Error class allows you to provide more meaningful information about the error. The Error class and its subclasses provide properties such as message and stack that can be used to convey useful details about the error, such as a description of the problem, the context in which it occurred, or a stack trace for debugging.

new Promise(function(resolve, reject) {
  reject(); // Noncompliant: use Error object to provide rejection reason
});

new Promise(function(resolve, reject) {
  reject('Something went wrong'); // Noncompliant: use Error object instead of literal
});

To fix your code provide an instance of the Error class to the promise reject function.

new Promise(function(resolve, reject) {
  reject(new Error('Network timeout'));
});

new Promise(function(resolve, reject) {
  reject(new Error('Something went wrong'));
});

name: Regular expressions should not cause non-linear backtracking

descriptionSections.content: Regular expression engines rely on backtracking to evaluate patterns against input. Certain regex patterns lead to non-linear backtracking, where the evaluation time grows polynomially with input size.

To fix a regular expression with non-linear backtracking, consider the following strategies:

  • Replace . with negated character classes to exclude separators where applicable (e.g., [^,]* instead of .* before ,).
  • Use bounded quantifiers such as {1,5} to limit repetitions.
  • Restructure alternations and quantifiers to eliminate ambiguity — avoid patterns where multiple alternatives can match the same character.
  • JavaScript does not support possessive quantifiers, but atomic grouping can be emulated using lookahead assertions and backreferences.
  • Use a non-backtracking implementation such as node-re2.

The following examples illustrate two distinct causes of non-linear backtracking. The first shows a pattern that is polynomial when unanchored: without a start anchor, the engine retries the pattern at every position, leading to quadratic evaluation time when there is no match. The second shows ambiguous alternation, which causes quadratic backtracking regardless of anchoring because multiple alternatives can match the same input in different ways.

Noncompliant code example

/a+b/.test(input); // Noncompliant - polynomial backtracking when the pattern does not match

/(a|aa)+/.test(input); // Noncompliant - ambiguous alternation causes quadratic backtracking

Compliant solution

Adding a start anchor prevents the engine from retrying at every position:

/^a+b/.test(input); // Compliant - anchor eliminates redundant backtracking positions

Restructuring the alternation to eliminate the overlap removes the quadratic behavior:

/a+/.test(input); // Compliant - unambiguous

Regular expression engines use backtracking to try all possible execution paths when evaluating a pattern against an input. In some cases, this leads to non-linear backtracking where the worst-case evaluation time grows polynomially (e.g., O(n²) or O(n³)) with the input size. While not as severe as catastrophic backtracking, such patterns can significantly degrade application performance when processing large or untrusted inputs.

This rule reports regular expressions that exhibit non-linear backtracking behavior.

Articles & blog posts

  • owasp.org - Regular expression Denial of Service - ReDoS
  • regular-expressions.info - Runaway Regular Expressions: Catastrophic Backtracking

Related rules

  • S5852 - Regular expressions should not cause catastrophic backtracking

name: "<button>" elements should have a valid "type" attribute, explicitly set when associated with a "<form>"

descriptionSections.content:
Documentation

  • MDN web docs - The <button> element - type attribute
  • HTML Standard - The button element - type
  • eslint-plugin-vue - Rule html-button-has-type
  • eslint-plugin-react - Rule button-has-type

A <button> element without an explicit type attribute defaults to type="submit" per the HTML Living Standard. When such a button is inside a <form>, clicking it can submit the form, even if that was not the developer’s intent. This is especially error-prone for buttons meant to trigger something other than submission, such as clearing a field or closing a dialog: without an explicit type, they can unexpectedly submit the enclosing form, potentially triggering an unwanted request or navigation.

A <button> can also be associated with a <form> it is not nested in, by referencing the form’s id through a form attribute; such a button is just as likely to trigger an unintended submission.

The HTML specification defines three valid type values for buttons: submit, reset, and button. A <button> with an invalid type value, e.g. type="action", is always flagged, regardless of whether the button is inside a <form>: the value is not a mistake that only matters in some contexts, and if the button is ever moved into a <form> or reused there, it silently falls back to the same unintended submit behavior described above.

Setting an explicit type on buttons inside a <form> or associated with one through a form attribute, and always using a valid value, removes this ambiguity and makes each button’s purpose explicit regardless of the browser rendering it.

This rule does not raise an issue for a missing type only when the <button> is neither inside a <form> nor associated with one through a form attribute, since there is then no submission to trigger. In React:

function Toolbar() {
  return <button>Menu</button>; // Compliant: not inside a <form> and has no "form" attribute
}

In a Vue template:

<template>
  <button>Menu</button> <!-- Compliant: not inside a <form> and has no "form" attribute -->
</template>

Noncompliant code example

function SearchForm() {
  return (
    <form action="/search">
      <input type="text" name="q" />
      <button>Search</button> // Noncompliant: defaults to type="submit"
      <button onClick={handleClear}>Clear</button> // Noncompliant: defaults to type="submit"
    </form>
  );
}

Compliant solution

function SearchForm() {
  return (
    <form action="/search">
      <input type="text" name="q" />
      <button type="submit">Search</button>
      <button type="button" onClick={handleClear}>Clear</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Noncompliant code example

<template>
  <button type="action">Save</button> <!-- Noncompliant: "action" is not a valid type -->
</template>

Compliant solution

<template>
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</template>

Noncompliant code example

<template>
  <form id="search" action="/search"></form>
  <button form="search">Clear</button> <!-- Noncompliant: defaults to type="submit" and submits the "search" form -->
</template>

Compliant solution

<template>
  <form id="search" action="/search"></form>
  <button form="search" type="button">Clear</button>
</template>

name: Promises should not be left unhandled

descriptionSections.content:
Documentation

  • typescript-eslint - Rule no-floating-promises
  • eslint-plugin-promise - Rule catch-or-return
  • MDN web docs - Promise
  • MDN web docs - Using promises
  • MDN web docs - void operator
  • Node.js Documentation - Event: 'unhandledRejection'

Related rules

  • S6544 - Promises should not be misused

A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. When a Promise is created but neither awaited, returned, nor given a rejection handler, it is said to be "floating": nothing in the code observes whether it eventually resolves or rejects.

This is a frequent source of bugs:

  • If the Promise rejects, nothing in the code reacts to the failure. The rejection escapes to the runtime’s global handler instead of the error handling around the call site, so recovery, retries, and user-facing messages never run.
  • Operations that were meant to happen in a specific order may instead run concurrently or out of order, because the code moved on before the asynchronous operation completed. Code that depends on the result may then execute too early, using stale or default data.
  • An array of Promises, such as the result of a map() call, is just as easy to leave unhandled as a single Promise, and is a common way to accidentally launch several operations without ever finding out if any of them failed.

This rule applies to Promise-valued statements. Promises used where another type is expected, such as in a conditional or a spread, are covered by S6544.

What is the potential impact?

An unhandled rejection is not contained to the operation that failed. Since Node.js 15, the default --unhandled-rejections mode is throw, which raises the rejection as an uncaught exception and terminates the process unless an unhandledRejection hook is registered. A single unobserved background task can therefore take down a server that was otherwise healthy.

Make sure every Promise-returning statement is handled in one of the following ways:

  • await it.
  • return it, so that the caller becomes responsible for handling it.
  • Attach a rejection handler with .catch(), or pass a rejection handler as the second argument to .then().
  • If you are dealing with several Promises at once, combine them with Promise.all(), Promise.allSettled(), Promise.race(), or Promise.any() before handling the result, instead of leaving an array of Promises unhandled.

If a Promise’s outcome genuinely does not matter and you want to make that explicit, use the void operator on the expression. This documents that the Promise is intentionally left unobserved. Note that this does not make rejections disappear: it only silences this rule, so it should be reserved for Promises that you know cannot practically reject, or that are otherwise covered by a global unhandled-rejection handler.

Noncompliant code example

function sendMetrics(payload) {
  fetch('/metrics', { method: 'POST', body: payload }); // Noncompliant: nothing handles a failed request
}

Compliant solution

async function sendMetrics(payload) {
  await fetch('/metrics', { method: 'POST', body: payload });
}

Noncompliant code example

function logAndForget() {
  fetchLogs().then(logs => storeLogs(logs)); // Noncompliant: no rejection handler
}

Compliant solution

function logAndForget() {
  fetchLogs()
    .then(logs => storeLogs(logs))
    .catch(error => reportError(error));
}

Noncompliant code example

function notifyAll(subscribers) {
  subscribers.map(subscriber => subscriber.notify()); // Noncompliant: an array of unhandled Promises
}

Compliant solution

async function notifyAll(subscribers) {
  await Promise.all(subscribers.map(subscriber => subscriber.notify()));
}

Noncompliant code example

function onClick() {
  trackEvent('button_clicked'); // Noncompliant: the Promise is left unhandled and is not marked as intentionally ignored
}

Compliant solution

function onClick() {
  // The analytics call is not expected to fail in a way that matters here.
  void trackEvent('button_clicked');
}
